title: A ten billion year stellar dance
caption: The globular cluster Messier 68, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: M 68 · constellation Hydra · about 35000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Stars crowd together in this Hubble view of Messier 68, a globular cluster, which is a spherical, star-filled region of space. In such clusters, the shared gravitational pull of hundreds of thousands, sometimes millions, of stars lets them survive as a group for many billions of years.

Astronomers can read a cluster's age in the light of its stars. Chemical elements leave signatures in starlight, and globular cluster stars usually contain less carbon, oxygen, iron and other heavy elements than stars like the Sun. Because successive generations of stars build up these elements through nuclear fusion, stars poor in them are relics of earlier times. Globular cluster stars rank among the oldest known, at more than 10 billion years.

More than 150 globular clusters surround the Milky Way, and on a galactic scale they are small. Messier 68's stars fill a volume little more than a hundred light-years across, while the Milky Way's disc stretches some 100 000 light-years or more.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.39 x 3.48 arcminutes) and distance (35000 light years), the frame spans roughly 35 × 35 light-years. Its light set out about 35,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and infrared exposures from the Wide Field Camera of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The infrared exposure records light the eye cannot see, and Hubble's sharp view separates the cluster's crowded stars.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: About 33 000 light-years from Earth, Messier 68 sits in the constellation Hydra, the Female Water Snake, and was the sixty-eighth entry in Charles Messier's catalog. The image combines visible and infrared light from the Advanced Camera for Surveys and covers about 3.4 by 3.4 arcminutes.
alt: A crowded, spherical cluster of stars.
